catalog_quote: There are three tonemes in Thok Reel High (H), Low (L) and High-Low (HL). Near-minimal pairs for tone are given in (87). In Thok Reel every syllable carries a tone, except perhaps the word-initial a- and ma- syllables (see (5) in section 3.3) which I have not studied in detail. Tone is used to distinguish lexical items (see 'night\SG' and 'dung\SG') and to signal morphological distinctions (all other examples in 87). [p. 119] ... In Thok Reel words are largely monosyllabic. This is a common characteristic of many Western Nilotic languages [p. 28] ... Whilst the majority of words are monosyllabic, there are also a small number of words with more than one syllable. These can be separated into three categories. First, there are native polysyllabic words (5a). The first syllable in such words can be a-, i-, è-, dàa-, and ma-. new_statements.rule_in_words: Thok Reel is described as a tone language (H, L, HL on every syllable, lexical and grammatical function, with word/phrase/sentence-level sandhi) whose roots are monosyllabic C(j/w)V(V)(V)C with three-way vowel length and a modal/breathy contrast; the description contains no statement of any kind about word stress or accent, and the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur in it.
new_statements.exceptions: Only tonal: word-initial a-/ma- syllables of the few native polysyllables may be toneless (not studied); no stress exceptions because no stress statement.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone on the (mostly monosyllabic) word; sandhi described at word, phrase and sentence level. Data from speakers of the Luac and Jilek sections (Rumbek/Yirol area).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Thok Reel (thɔk rɛ̈ɛ̈l, 'Atuot/Atwot' is the Dinka exonym) = Glottolog reel1238 / ISO atu. Reid 2010's consultants are from the Luac and Jilek sections (Rumbek and Yirol, Lakes State); she notes possible idiolect/dialect differences in tone-rule ordering between two speakers. The SIL books (2015-2016) were produced with Reel speakers in Juba workshops and cite Reid 2010 as their linguistic basis.
